speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Both Al-Qaeda and ISIS-related terrorists have identified Singapore as a target, along with Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The ongoing Marawi crisis in southern Philippines indicates that extremist terrorism is now endemic in this region and it may take many years before that security problem is rooted out.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Foreign fighters from countries like Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Chechnya were reported to be fighting in Marawi and more are expected to join them, including returning fighters from this region who are now in Iraq and Syria.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Their stated goal is to establish a wilayat, or a province of the caliphate, supported by global terrorist financing and networks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Stashes of weapons, ammunition and large amounts of cash amounting to millions of dollars have reportedly been discovered during raids of terrorist camps in Marawi.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If these terrorist cells are entrenched deeper in Mindanao or any part of ASEAN, they will launch attacks against our people in Singapore and other cities in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We must do all we can to prevent this from happening, to keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: MINDEF and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) take this extremist threat to Singapore and Singaporeans very seriously and we have been making changes to deal with it decisively at various levels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: First, to counter the terrorism threat at its source.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This requires an international effort and the SAF has been part of the coalition against jihadi terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF was in Afghanistan from 2007 to 2013 against Al-Qaeda, our longest overseas deployment to date, with close to 500 personnel deployed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Since 2015, the SAF has also deployed units as part of the multinational coalition efforts against ISIS.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These deployments included Intelligence Fusion Officers, Imagery Analysts and air-to-air refuelling tanker aircraft to various parts of the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Right now, we have an SAF medical team in Iraq as an ongoing part of this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Second, we need to deal with geographically proximate threats in our region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If we wait till the problem comes onto our shores, for terrorists to attack us here before we respond, it will be too little, too late.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For this reason, Singapore encouraged strongly the three littoral states − Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines − to initiate the Trilateral Maritime Patrol in the Sulu Seas and offered the help of the Republic of Singapore Navy's Information Fusion Centre to facilitate information-sharing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF stands ready to assist in these patrols when invited.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: MINDEF has been informed that President Duterte has accepted in principle Singapore's offer of assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Details of the implementation are now being worked out.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Third, we must strengthen our defences at home, not only to respond to terrorist attacks but to prevent radicalisation of our own people and deal with the social consequences in the aftermath of attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We set up four task forces dedicated to homeland security − the Special Operations Task Force, the Maritime Security Task Force (MSTF), the Air Defence Task Force (ADTF) and the Island Defence Task Force.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our sailors, soldiers and airmen in these task forces conduct 24/7 operations to keep our air, land and seas secure.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In recent years, in responding to the evolving threat from ISIS-related terrorists, further changes have been made to equip and train many more SAF personnel to deal with these threats effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Island Defence Training Institute (IDTI) was opened yesterday by Second Minister for Defence Ong Ye Kung.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And the IDTI will prepare active and National Service (NS) units to undertake Homeland Defence and Security Operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will equip soldiers with the necessary competencies to be deployed alongside their counterparts from MHA.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Soldiers will go through video simulation training to hone their thinking processes and application of Rules of Engagement, which include scenarios, such as coastal patrols, security checkpoints and the like.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Beyond these organisational changes, the SAF has also systematically updated its tactics, techniques and procedures for counter-terrorism operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are now purchasing more new equipment that will provide SAF forces better mobility, more accurate situational assessments and precise capabilities to neutralise terrorists in urban settings when they strike there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our soldiers will use more unmanned systems to improve surveillance and responses.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF will also enhance our air and sea defences.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The ADTF stays sharp with regular Exercise Vigilance exercises and drills.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF and the Home Team are working well together and closer to deal with the terrorism threat.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have instituted a regular exercise framework to test and validate our joint operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: One example is the joint counter-terrorism exercise which aims to validate joint counter-terrorism plans in October last year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Engineers from DSTA and DSO National Laboratories are using data analytics technologies to pick up specific threats and provide early warning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will there be more joint exercises between the Home Team and SAF to help ensure that both forces synergise their efforts and arsenal against the threat of terrorism?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will there be a joint response from both forces should a terrorist threat, unfortunately, vest on our shores?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Traditionally, I think, neither the home teams of countries nor the SAF, or rather the military in that sense, were geared up to deal with terrorism on this scale.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we have seen it in various scenarios: whether it is a truck that mows down innocent pedestrians; whether it is at the airport; whether it is in crowded places, we are not structured that way.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And when you have multiple attacks, as occurred in France, you find security agencies having to mobilise beyond what the first line of defenders have to do, when their needs or demands are overwhelmed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that is, indeed, a clear recognition that you have to prepare for these scenarios.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It could be very small, it could be much larger.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And across that spectrum, how do you scale up, scale down?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do you respond effectively, how do you coordinate effectively?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You cannot wait and say, "Well, let something happen then we learn." The closest we can get is through, exactly as the Member says, different exercise scenarios.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even before that, we need to coordinate planning considerations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do you have a common understanding between the Home Team and the SAF, recognising that the Home Team are the first responders because they are in society and that has been their role?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I would say that there is a clear recognition that we need to exercise more often together and, indeed, we have.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I talked about also an exercise in the maritime domain with different agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we are aware of this need to coordinate and integrate our responses, not only of our security agencies, but of our community groups.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because, as I have said, while our security teams and security agencies can exercise, what we need to pay attention to is the aftermath of attacks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And, Madam, I think that is a whole-of-society response.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share − apart from Singapore – which countries have contributed resources to the military effort in the Philippines against ISIS elements?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It very much depends on what the AFP says it needs and the relationships that the Philippines have with other militaries and other countries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From what we know, a number of countries have been reported to be helping the Philippines, such as the United States.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you consider the Trilateral Maritime Patrol in the Sulu Seas, which the Philippines does with Malaysia and Indonesia, then Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members may have read that Malaysia also mobilised a humanitarian plane, under the auspices of AHA, which is the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Practically in every household, you will find a National Serviceman.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How could the Government leverage on this advantage that we have to work with the community to form a strong defence against terrorism?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think there are clear roles that security agencies should do because that is the primary responsibility and we have to have community groups.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As members of the security forces, I think the public rightly expects the Home Team, the SAF − whether they are National Servicemen or Regulars − to be able to protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You cannot just say, "Well, go and protect Singaporeans." And that was the essence of launching the IDTI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I mentioned this institute and you may have seen footages yesterday in the news.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not easy to tell someone with arms and, sometimes, you are worried that, "If you think this person is going to harm somebody else, if he is a terrorist, neutralise him." Because you can make the wrong judgement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In a tensed situation, the outcome can become very negative.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have basically video simulation screens which are life-size and moving targets − which means people, some are "hostages" and you also have "terrorists".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if they make the wrong decision, in an instant, they will know it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have to get them used to that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not think they can be as proficient as the average policeman because that is not what they do every day but, at least you have that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And also, in the change of our assets, how we are equipping for that, we have mentioned that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But at the community level, Mr Gan's question is: how do you ensure that we can protect at the precinct level?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I think that is not only for NSmen who are from the SAF, Home Team or SCDF which they have some level of training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think that is where many of our community exercises are now dealing with it − emergency preparedness, where you bring in communities and you have to respond.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think there is great scope and need for our community agencies to come together.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know that many Members, including myself, have been doing this − bringing community leaders and saying, "When we have an attack, can I depend on you for these resources?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Can I depend on you to calm the community down, to speak to the community?" And I think we need to continually do that.
